bibl.title: Political Discourse on Social Media: Echo Chambers, Gatekeepers, and the Price of Bipartisanship

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: existence
span.quote: When applied to discussions about politically contentious topics, our results support the existence of political echo chambers.

span.label: political echo chambers on social media
span.quote: This paper studies the phenomenon of political echo chambers on social media.

span.label: observational-data-analysis
span.quote: We use a collection of ten different datasets from Twitter, each of which contains a set of tweets on a given topic of discussion.

span.label: political leaning is measured only from tweets that link to news sources of known, independently-derived leaning, not the message content itself
span.quote: To quantify the political leaning of content posted on Twitter, we consider only messages that contain a link to an online news organization with a known and independently derived political leaning.

span.label: All data come from Twitter and are only a sample of social-media discussion.
span.quote: First, the datasets used are just a sample of all the discussions in social media, and they all come from Twitter.

span.label: Results are drawn from politically-savvy users and should not be assumed to generalise to the general public.
span.quote: However, as we focused on politically-savvy users on Twitter, the reader should not infer that our observations generalize immediately to other settings, or that echo chamber effects are as pronounced for the general public.

span.label: The polarity measures depend on externally supplied political labels for news sources.
span.quote: Second, our production and consumption scores rely on external labeling of news sources along a political axis.

span.label: Following is used as a proxy for actual consumption; users may not read everything their neighbours post.
span.quote: Moreover, our analysis assumes that each user consumes all content produced by all their neighbors.

span.label: Some articles from the scored news domains may not be political.
span.quote: Finally, it is possible that not all news articles from the news sources we base the polarity measures are political.

span.label: The causal relations between selective exposure, biased assimilation, algorithmic filtering and echo chambers are not addressed.
span.quote: Understanding how all these phenomena interact with each other and the precise causality relations is beyond the scope of this paper.

span.label: The literature has no consensus definition of the paper's central term, so the authors chose one.
span.quote: As there is no consensus on a formal definition in the literature, we opt for this definition, which is general enough and reasonably captures the essence of the phenomenon

span.label: A term is borrowed from another field with its unit of analysis changed, which the authors state.
span.quote: Gatekeepers are defined in media and communication studies as media sources that act as filters (or ‘gatekeepers’) of information [27]. In our case, we consider consumption and production of content jointly, and define gatekeepers as users who consume content from both sides of the political spectrum but only produce content from one side

span.label: A second definition of the same category was tested and its results not presented.
span.quote: We also experimented with a different definition of gatekeepers – users who have a high consumption variance and low production variance. This definition captures a slightly broader set of users (compared to Equation 5), e.g., users who consume from both ends of the political spectrum and produce balanced ‘centrist’ content. The results were almost identical to the ones reported above in Section 5.3, and so we do not present them explicitly

span.label: What the identified users are actually doing is left open by the authors.
span.quote: Nevertheless, from our current analysis, it is not clear if such users act as open-minded net-citizens

span.label: an echo chamber - AS AGREEMENT BETWEEN TWO PER-USER SCORES: it exists, for this paper, when the leaning of the content a user receives agrees with the leaning of what they share; not a group, not a network structure, not an isolation measure, but a correlation computed per user - and the authors adopt it because the literature offers no consensus formal definition to inherit
span.quote: We say that an echo chamber exists if the political leaning of the content that users receive from the network agrees with that of the content they share. As there is no consensus on a formal definition in the literature, we opt for this definition, which is general enough and reasonably captures the essence of the phenomenon

span.label: a gatekeeper - AN INDIVIDUAL USER, NOT A MEDIA SOURCE: communication studies gives the word to institutions that filter what passes into a channel, and this paper reassigns it to a person at a particular position on two scores, stating the earlier sense and supplying a bridging argument - that such users block information from one side, and hence can be considered gatekeepers
span.quote: Gatekeepers are defined in media and communication studies as media sources that act as filters (or ‘gatekeepers’) of information [27]. In our case, we consider consumption and production of content jointly, and define gatekeepers as users who consume content from both sides of the political spectrum but only produce content from one side. These users block or filter information from one side, and hence can be considered gatekeepers

span.label: leaning - A STIPULATED SCORE, WITH ITS OWN SYNONYMS NAMED IN THE FOOTNOTE THAT STIPULATES IT: the authors define it as a score quantifying alignment with one political side and list the terms the literature uses for the same thing, so four words - leaning, ideology, polarity, ideological stance - are declared interchangeable by the paper itself
span.quote: as a score that quantifies alignment with one political side. Similar terms in the literature include “ideology,” “polarity,” or “ideological stance

span.label: extends → the study of political polarization and echo chambers
span.quote: The results shown in this study are just one step towards the understanding of echo chambers and the interplay between network and content, which open up several directions for future work.

span.label: builds-on → the latent space model of Barberá et al. [7]
span.quote: We adopt the latent space model proposed by Barberá et al. [7] to estimate a user polarity score.

span.label: builds-on → the news-source leaning scores and hard/soft news classifier of Bakshy et al. [4]
span.quote: During preprocessing, we attempted to split news articles from these sources into hard (politics, opinion, etc.) and soft news (gossip, entertainment, etc.) and applied the classifier from Bakshy et al. [4].

span.label: replicates → Barberá [6] on higher polarization of retweet networks for political topics
span.quote: This result reinforces the validity of the proposed measures — and agrees with similar conclusions presented by Barberá [6], where retweet networks exhibit higher polarization for political topics.

span.label: extends → prior echo-chamber studies that measure either content or network alone
span.quote: In this paper, we propose measures to identify the existence of an echo chamber by using both the content being read/shared and the network that enables the content to propagate.

span.label: echo chamber —operationalised-as→ leaning
span.quote: We say that an echo chamber exists if the political leaning of the content that users receive from the network agrees with that of the content they share. As there is no consensus on a formal definition in the literature, we opt for this definition, which is general enough and reasonably captures the essence of the phenomenon

span.label: gatekeeper —contrasted-with→ media sources
span.quote: Gatekeepers are defined in media and communication studies as media sources that act as filters (or ‘gatekeepers’) of information [27]. In our case, we consider consumption and production of content jointly, and define gatekeepers as users who consume content from both sides of the political spectrum but only produce content from one side

span.label: Studying political echo chambers on Twitter via a production-vs-consumption measure of users political leaning, users are largely exposed to opinions agreeing with their own — confirming echo chambers.
span.quote: By comparing the two, we find that Twitter users are, to a large degree, exposed to political opinions that agree with their own.

span.label: Exposure is measured at three levels — production (what a user shares), consumption (what appears in their feed), and engagement (what they click).
span.quote: engagement, which includes all content that a user clicks

span.label: content production vs consumption political leaning
span.term: content production vs consumption political leaning
span.quote: We define a production and consumption measure for social-media users, which captures the political leaning of the content shared and received by them

span.label: exposure to agreeing vs opposing opinions (echo-chamber strength)
span.term: exposure to agreeing vs opposing opinions (echo-chamber strength)
span.quote: Twitter users are, to a large degree, exposed to political opinions that agree with their own

span.label: production / consumption / engagement measures

span.label: effect-size
span.quote: Finally, their tweets are more appreciated, i.e., a higher fraction of their tweets receives a retweet, albeit the effect size is smaller in this case (figure not shown).
